summary: Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) is a piperazine-derivative antifilarial used to treat lymphatic filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi/timori), loiasis (Loa loa) and tropical pulmonary eosinophilia. It rapidly clears microfilariae and has macrofilaricidal activity against some species. It is NOT FDA-approved and in the United States is available only through the CDC; dosing follows WHO/CDC guidance. The major hazards are severe inflammatory (Mazzotti-type) reactions from dying parasites - serious encephalopathy in heavy Loa loa loads and worsened eye disease in onchocerciasis - so DEC is avoided in onchocerciasis and used cautiously in high-burden loiasis.

moa: Diethylcarbamazine's exact mechanism is not fully defined. It is thought to immobilize microfilariae by altering their surface membranes, making them susceptible to host immune destruction, and to interfere with arachidonic-acid metabolism in both the parasite and host vascular endothelium, promoting clearance of microfilariae from the circulation. It also has activity against adult worms of some filarial species.

absolute: Onchocerciasis (risk of severe Mazzotti reaction and ocular damage)
monitor: Ocular examination if onchocerciasis is possible

preg: Avoid during pregnancy. Treatment is generally deferred until after delivery because safety is not established and treatment-related reactions could harm the pregnancy.
lact: Limited data on excretion in human milk; use with caution and weigh benefit against potential infant exposure.
renal: DEC and its metabolites are excreted renally and excretion is reduced (and half-life prolonged) in renal impairment and with alkaline urine; reduce the dose or extend the interval and use caution.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; specific adjustment data are limited.

pearls: NOT FDA-approved - in the US it is available only through the CDC; dosing follows WHO/CDC protocols
Do NOT give in onchocerciasis - severe Mazzotti reactions and irreversible ocular damage can result (use ivermectin instead)
In loiasis, very high Loa loa microfilarial loads can trigger fatal encephalopathy - quantify the load and escalate the dose slowly
Post-treatment fever/itch/adenopathy are reactions to dying parasites, not drug allergy - pre-treat with antihistamines/steroids
Renal excretion is slowed by alkaline urine, raising drug levels
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered on the same day; if it is nearly time for the next dose, skip it and resume the schedule. Do not double up. Follow the specific program/CDC schedule, which may escalate doses over the first days.
overdose: Experience is limited; overdose would be expected to intensify gastrointestinal and inflammatory reactions and CNS effects (dizziness, headache). Management is supportive - antihistamines and corticosteroids for severe reactions, fluids and antiemetics as needed, and monitoring for neurologic deterioration, especially in loiasis.
